parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State **two** advantages of the transmission of data in digital, rather than analogue, form.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem:
An analogue signal is to be transmitted in digital form.

The transmission system may be represented in block form as in Fig. 4.1.

{{figure:figure_4_1.png}}

The variation with time $t$ of part of the input analogue signal is shown in Fig. 4.2.

{{figure:figure_4_2.png}}

The analogue signal is sampled at time intervals of $0.10\text{ ms}$. The first sample is taken at time $t = 0$.

Some values of the sampled analogue signal and the corresponding digital signals are shown in Table 4.1.

Each digitised number contains four bits.

Table 4.1

| {{header}} time $t / \text{ms}$ | {{header}} 0 | {{header}} 0.10 | {{header}} 0.20 | {{header}} 0.30 | {{header}} 0.40 | {{header}} 0.50 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| analogue signal / $\text{mV}$ | 0 | 5.7 | 6.2 | {{answer}} | {{answer}} | {{answer}} |
| digital signal | 0000 | 0101 | 0110 | {{answer}} | {{answer}} | {{answer}} |

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: In Table 4.1, underline the least significant bit (LSB) in the digital signal for the time of $0.20\text{ ms}$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
A single bit from the output of the digital-to-analogue converter corresponds to an output analogue signal of $1.0\text{ mV}$.

Assume that the conversion and transmission do not introduce a time delay.

On the axes of Fig. 4.3, show the variation with time $t$ of the output from the digital-to-analogue converter.

{{figure:figure_4_3.png}}
